script.title: How a Chess Machine Hid a Human Master for 84 Years
sentences: A machine in a turban won most of its chess games.
Wolfgang von Kempelen built it in 1770 to impress Empress Maria Theresa.
Before games he opened every door to show the gears.
He let a big magnet sit by the board, to show magnetism played no part.
Its opponents included Napoleon Bonaparte and Benjamin Franklin.
One old lady hid in a window seat, sure an evil spirit lived inside.
Actually a chess master sat inside on a sliding seat, working the arm with levers.
The first full explanation came in 1857, after a fire had destroyed it.
script.description:
An 18th-century chess automaton toured Europe for 84 years.
The player was a person hidden inside.
visuals: The Turk chess automaton Kempelen engraving
claims_en: The Mechanical Turk was a chess-playing machine first displayed in 1770.
The model was dressed in Ottoman robes and a turban.
Wolfgang von Kempelen constructed it to impress Empress Maria Theresa, completing it in early 1770.
Kempelen began every showing by opening the doors and drawers of the cabinet, exposing gears and cogs.
Kempelen would often allow a large magnet to sit at the side of the board to show the machine was not influenced by magnetism.
It played games against Napoleon Bonaparte and Benjamin Franklin.
Von Windisch wrote of an old lady who hid in a window seat, believing an evil spirit possessed the machine.
A chess master hidden inside moved the pieces via levers and magnets.
A sliding seat let the operator move and evade observation.
The operator moved the Turk's arm with a lever mechanism (pantograph).
It was destroyed in a fire in 1854.
In 1857 an article by the owner's son gave the first full explanation of the mechanism.
It was exhibited as an automaton for 84 years.
